pr_body:
Replaces: #22391 #22066

Implements what is discussed here:

https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/22391#issuecomment-1040092633
pr_comments: /cc @medhefgo @keszybz

> I still don't like it for the very same reason outlined in the previous discussion.

Which specific reason do you mean? Can you elaborate?

> This also doesn't fix the `arch-lts.conf` vs `arch.conf` case either (I will consider reverting my commit without a fix for this a regression).

It doesn't? Why not? Arch can choose any sorting order they want, by carefully picking a sort-key. for example, they could use `sort-key archlinux-30` and `sort-key archlinux-70` or so in the entry they want to order explicitly against each other. sort-key gives them explicit control what should come first

> Which specific reason do you mean? Can you elaborate?

Just re-read that PR. I don't feel like repeating myself.

> It doesn't? Why not? Arch can choose any sorting order they want, by carefully picking a sort-key. for example, they could use `sort-key archlinux-30` and `sort-key archlinux-70` or so in the entry they want to order explicitly against each other. sort-key gives them explicit control what should come first

That's not the point. Your PR does not sort entries the way people expect it to, and they shouldn't have to resort to using sort-key for this just because it fails to ignore the file ending when sorting. Even worse, sorting by sort-key vs without creates a list order that makes no sense (as I have explained above) and even confuses the default entry selection algorithm.

I think maybe the right approach is decoupling the entry sorting from default/priority selection...

> This allows snippet generators to explicitly order entries: any string can be set as an entry's "sort key". If set, sd-boot will use it to sort entries on display.

> New logic is hence (ignore the boot counting logic)

>  sort-key is set → primary sort key: sort-key (lexicographically increasing order)
>                   → secondary sort key: machine-id (also increasing order)
>                   → tertiary sort key: version (lexicographically decreasing order!)

>   sort-key is not set → primary sort key: entry filename (aka id), lexicographically increasing order)

> With this scheme we can order OSes by their names from A-Z but then put within the same OS still the newest version first. This should clean up the order to match expectations more.

This doesn't sound right. If sort-key is the most important thing set, then it'd mean that distributions would need to somehow use different sort-key prefixes or entries from different distributions would interleave. And with parallel installations of the same distro things would be even worse. It seems that machine-id (in the sense of about-to-be-renamed KERNEL_INSTALL_MACHINE_ID) must be the primary sorting key.

As @medhefgo showed above, entries with and without sort-key cannot be compared. In particular, *adding* or *removing* an entry could cause some other entries to reverse order. The only solution that preserves transitivity is to sort entries without sort-key either as always earlier or later than those with sort-key. Since sort-key is "new", it seems reasonable to sort all such entries later.

Also having a sort-key order that is reverse of the version order sounds just terrible. The natural thing would be to generate entries with "version: someprefix-nnn-somepostfix, sort-key: maybeotherprefix-nnn". Let's just sort in alphanumerical order like with versions.

Sorry, but this seems to make the situation much worse.

> This doesn't sound right. If sort-key is the most important thing set, then it'd mean that distributions would need to somehow use different sort-key prefixes or entries from different distributions would interleave.

Hmm? Yes that's the point, Fedora would set the sort key to "fedora", and Arch to "arch". 

> And with parallel installations of the same distro things would be even worse. It seems that machine-id (in the sense of about-to-be-renamed KERNEL_INSTALL_MACHINE_ID) must be the primary sorting key.

if you have parallel installations of the same distro, then they' have the same sort key, but different machine ID, so we'd group them by machine ID.

Not sure where the confusion is? How would *you* sort the stuff? I don#t follow at all anymore.

> As @medhefgo showed above, entries with and without sort-key cannot be compared.

I cannot parse this. the patch follows the logic that either we have two "new-style" entries that both have a sort key set, in which case it is used for comparisons. Or one or both lack it, in which case we revert to the status quo ante, and just use the id. What#s wrong with that? I don#t follow what you are requesting instead?

> > This doesn't sound right. If sort-key is the most important thing set, then it'd mean that distributions would need to somehow use different sort-key prefixes or entries from different distributions would interleave.
> 
> Hmm? Yes that's the point, Fedora would set the sort key to "fedora", and Arch to "arch".

Oh, OK. So you want to use the sort-key to distinguish between e.g. "distros", and then the ~machine-id to distinguish between installations, and finally version to order different kernel versions for the same installation. OK, makes sense.

My comment about comparing versions with the key and without also can be ignored.

But the part about non-transitive sorting still stands.

> Also having a sort-key order that is reverse of the version order sounds just terrible. The natural thing would be to generate entries with "version: someprefix-nnn-somepostfix, sort-key: maybeotherprefix-nnn". Let's just sort in alphanumerical order like with versions.

Can't parse this either. Are you saying you want Arch appear after or before Fedora in the list? And do you want that version 5 of Arch shall be placed after or before versin 6 of Arch? I assumed people want that Arch is before Fedora, And Arch 6 before ARch 5. But you want something else?

I know for a fact that I am confused now. I have the suspicion that I might not be the only one though?

hmm, so you are concerned about cases where a triplet of entries with IDs X, Y, Z of which Y has no sort key but X and Z have sort-keys "B" and "A"?

In that case if one compares Y with X and Z one would assume an order X, Y, Z but if one compares X with Z one would assume an order Z, X (due to the sort keys)? And those two orders are contradictory?

That indeed is a problem. Not sure what the right fix is for that though.

> I cannot parse this. the patch follows the logic that either we have two "new-style" entries that both have a sort key set, in which case it is used for comparisons. Or one or both lack it, in which case we revert to the status quo ante, and just use the id. What#s wrong with that? I don#t follow what you are requesting instead?

So imagine that we are transitioning to this scheme, and we have an entry
```
machine-id A
version 1
title A-1
```
and we add a new entry with
```
machine-id B
sort-key 11
title B-11
```
they will be sorted A, B-11.
And then we add
```
machine-id A
sort-key 12
version 2
title A-12
```
and they will be sorted A-12 < A-1 < B-11.
And then you remove A-1 on upgrade, and they are sorted B-11 < A-12.

I'm requesting instead that we sort anything with sort-key as higher priority then anything w/o. (On the assumption that entries with sort-key are newer.)

Thus B-11, A-12, A-1 first, and then B-11, A-12 when A-1 is removed.

I can't quite figure this out with the current code, but the general principle should be that in the boot menu, entries with later versions are sorted towards the top of the screen. And to keep user sanity, the output from bootctl should have the same visual order as the sd-boot menu:

With this patch I see the following:
```
$ build/bootctl list
Boot Loader Entries:
         type: Boot Loader Specification Type #1 (.conf)
        title: Fedora Linux 35 (Workstation Edition Prerelease) (default) (not reported/new)
           id: 08a5690a2eed47cf92ac0a5d2e3cf6b0-5.14.9-300.fc35.x86_64.conf
       source: /boot/efi/loader/entries/08a5690a2eed47cf92ac0a5d2e3cf6b0-5.14.9-300.fc35.x86_64.conf
      version: 5.14.9-300.fc35.x86_64
   machine-id: 08a5690a2eed47cf92ac0a5d2e3cf6b0
        linux: /08a5690a2eed47cf92ac0a5d2e3cf6b0/5.14.9-300.fc35.x86_64/linux
       initrd: /08a5690a2eed47cf92ac0a5d2e3cf6b0/5.14.9-300.fc35.x86_64/initrd
      options: ...

         type: Boot Loader Specification Type #1 (.conf)
        title: Fedora Linux 35 (Workstation Edition) (selected) (not reported/new)
           id: 08a5690a2eed47cf92ac0a5d2e3cf6b0-5.15.14-200.fc35.x86_64.conf
       source: /boot/efi/loader/entries/08a5690a2eed47cf92ac0a5d2e3cf6b0-5.15.14-200.fc35.x86_64.conf
      version: 5.15.14-200.fc35.x86_64
   machine-id: 08a5690a2eed47cf92ac0a5d2e3cf6b0
        linux: /08a5690a2eed47cf92ac0a5d2e3cf6b0/5.15.14-200.fc35.x86_64/linux
       initrd: /08a5690a2eed47cf92ac0a5d2e3cf6b0/5.15.14-200.fc35.x86_64/initrd
      options: ...
```
and when I boot with this sd-boot version, it also uses the same order, and selects the older version.

> I hate sorting by filenames when it should be done by content (this applies to userspace too)?

FWIW, I'm with @poetting on this one. We shouldn't sort on content, because this just too fragile. Any time you append " (prerelease)" or " (final)" or change anything in the wording of the title you risk getting the wrong sort order.

> Hmm, but why the `if`?
> This should just be:

*I* would *love* that. I'll leave the why this would be against what the two of you want as an exercise to the reader. :P
Hmm, did I say that somewhere?

> FWIW, I'm with @poetting on this one..

> Hmm, did I say that somewhere?

Without that if you are comparing the *contents*, which you said you don't want.

> Thins means that we'd compare two images with no sort key and no machine id by their version id, but that's hardly comparable...

So, previously the "version" field of entries where "local" to the OS, i.e. only was used to distinguish two entries of the *same* OS install. With the suggested comparison this would change, we'd suddenly order by that *before* sorting by OS. 

so, previously an entry with entry fname of "fedora-23.conf" that lacks both sort-key and machine id (but has a version 23 field), would be ordered after "arch-17.conf" that also lacks both sort-key and machine id (but has a version 17 field). But with your proposed series of comparisons, we'd suddenly compare them by version only, i.e. suddenly fedora-23.conf would be placed *before* fedora-17.conf, because it is newer.

So I think we should do what zbigniew originally suggested: put new-style entries that have a sort key before old style entries that do not. Yes, this will mean things are reordered during the transition where everyone adds sort key fields, but things are very systematic, and ordering is transitive, as requested.

You still haven't addressed things?

I fail to see how the comparison function is transitive. Unless you think that calling it "hardly comparable" (== undefined behavior in c spec parlance) is enough??

And I still don't see how you plan to address the inconsistent default entry selection when you have this mixed sorting. Entries with sort-key are sorted *ascending* and selected/preferred in that order, while old entries are sorted *descending* and selected/preferred in *reverse* order). *This makes no sense*. And you will get people complaining about [*that*](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/22004).

> You still haven't addressed things?

Adressed which things?

> I fail to see how the comparison function is transitive. Unless you think that calling it "hardly comparable" (== undefined behavior in c spec parlance) is enough??

If we always port entries with a sort key before those without we basically partition the set of entries in two, and then order only inside each of the two subset. And inside each subset the ordering is entirely systematic, i.e. we only consider an entry property for sorting if all more important ones are entirely identical (which means also both set or both unset). Thus the ordering of three entries A, B, C where A < C also means A < B and B < C, and that's what we need for transitivity.

> And I still don't see how you plan to address the inconsistent default entry selection when you have this mixed sorting. Entries with sort-key are sorted _ascending_ and selected/preferred in that order, while old entries are sorted _descending_ and selected/preferred in _reverse_ order). _This makes no sense_. And you will get people complaining about [_that_](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/22004).

In the new world order (i.e. where evrything has a sort key) everything is clean and works as it should. In the old world order (where things do not have a sort key) things will remain as before. If both worlds are mixed, then the new wold order comes first. This together means behaviour should be quite OK I think.

Yes, it means during the transition things will be ordered sometimes in suprising ways, but still in a completely systematic ways. And I think people might not even notice the transition as after all kernel-install now implicitly generates new-style entries, thus old style enrties should go away sooner or later.

I see. Your approach is putting your head in the sands and pretend this is not messed up. :roll_eyes:

> If we always port entries with a sort key before those without we basically partition the set of entries in two, and then order only inside each of the two subset. And inside each subset the ordering is entirely systematic, i.e. we only consider an entry property for sorting if all more important ones are entirely identical (which means also both set or both unset). Thus the ordering of three entries A, B, C where A < C also means A < B and B < C, and that's what we need for transitivity.

Except it doesn't? As stated before A < B < C *and* C < A:
```
A: id=a.conf sort-key=50
B: id=b.conf
C: id=c.conf sort-key=40
```

> Yes, it means during the transition things will be ordered sometimes in suprising ways, but still in a completely systematic ways. And I think people might not even notice the transition as after all kernel-install now implicitly generates new-style entries, thus old style enrties should go away sooner or later.

As the linked issue shows, people will notice and and get grumpy over it. And expecting a kernel update to coincide with sd-boot seems overly optimistic for me.

Also, what about users that don't use kernel-install and expect their ordering to be correct? They might even be using boot counting, but *that* will end up preferring/selecting a *bad* entry now if one exists.

> Except it doesn't? As stated before A < B < C _and_ C < A:
> 
> ```
> A: id=a.conf sort-key=50
> B: id=b.conf
> C: id=c.conf sort-key=40
> ```

According to @keszybz' original suggestion we'd put those first that have a sort key, and those last that do not. Thus the order would be C, A, B. And regardless which pair of these you'll compare it will always match this order. i.e. A < B (because A has a sort key, and B does not), C < A (because both have a sort key and 40 < 50), C < B (because C has a sort key and B has not).

So it's fully transitive. All good!

> Also, what about users that don't use kernel-install and expect their ordering to be correct? They might even be using boot counting, but _that_ will end up preferring/selecting a _bad_ entry now if one exists.

I don't follow at all: your patch switched things over to using the human readable title for sorting, which suddenly reordered everything for everyone, because a completely different string was now used for sorting that wasn't put together with sort order in mind at all? I mean any kind of sort order change isn't ideal. Your change isn't in any way better than this one. If you have a problem with changing hte sort order, then we should revert to the status quo ante. I don't follow anymore at all?

> According to @keszybz' original suggestion we'd put those first that have a sort key, and those last that do not. Thus the order would be C, A, B. And regardless which pair of these you'll compare it will always match this order. i.e. A < B (because A has a sort key, and B does not), C < A (because both have a sort key and 40 < 50), C < B (because C has a sort key and B has not).
> 
> So it's fully transitive. All good!

I don't see that being done in your comparison function. The list will not be magically in this order or you wouldn't need to sort it in the first place.
(And regardless of whether it makes sense or not, you still need to also make sure the sorting within sort-key entries is transitive too, even if they lack a version or machine-id field.)

> I don't follow at all: your patch switched things over to using the human readable title for sorting, which suddenly reordered everything for everyone, because a completely different string was now used for sorting that wasn't put together with sort order in mind at all? I mean any kind of sort order change isn't ideal. Your change isn't in any way better than this one. If you have a problem with changing hte sort order, then we should revert to the status quo ante. I don't follow anymore at all?

True, I give you that. But your ordering is seems rather inconsistent to me (particularly regarding the default selection). And that  goes doubly so during a transition period.

> I don't see that being done in your comparison function. The list will not be magically in this order or you wouldn't need to sort it in the first place.

No, not in the one I original pushed. But @keszybz original proposal was different to what I suggested. he suggested to systematically put entries that have a sort key before those which do not. I have not implemented that yet, I am just arguing, that that's the right approach, in my eyes, now. Will push a patch for that shortly.
Also, you may wanna make sure https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/22580 is fixed while you're at it.
Force pushed a new version now. PTAL.

The new version includes a simple new test that checks if the order matches the expectations.

This does not fix #22580, which is unrelated. Fix for that one should be simple, but let's do that in another PR.

I am still sorely missing ignoring the `.efi/.conf` part of the id. And it probably makes to ignore the boot counting part of the file name too for the same reason (and it's already being explicitly dealt with anyways).
(This needs to be rebased.)

> I am still sorely missing ignoring the `.efi/.conf` part of the id. And it probably makes to ignore the boot counting part of the file name too for the same reason (and it's already being explicitly dealt with anyways).

Yeah the boot counting we definitely should drop, but I think that's a separate issue. I'd consider that a separate issue though. I'll add a TODO list item for it.

(That said, for entries with a sort-key removing the boot count from the id is not that important...)
Force pushed a new rebased version, with the compariso changes @medhefgo suggested. PTAL.

You'd imho still want entries with sort-key to go before entries without one. Which this fails to do.
I am not convinced that's desirable. I'd rather stick to the traditional sorting if we cannot compare by sort key.

That create an "unstable" sorting order. Realistically, you cannot compare entries with to entries without. You're comparing apples vs oranges in that case, so ignoring the fact and resorting to comparing by color next makes no sense.

To put this in more concrete terms, your sorting function is violating transitivity.

Given this list:
```
1: id=a.conf sort-key=50
2: id=b.conf
3: id=c.conf sort-key=40
```

You have these realtions:
```
1 < 2 (id)
2 < 3 (id)
```

Which by transitivity must imply `1 < 3`, but it doesn't because `1 > 3 (sort-key) !!!`

This means that depending on the original order of the list, you can generate an unstable sorting output.
